not_covered: A US court found Google’s search business to be a monopoly because it violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by engaging in exclusionary conduct through default-distribution deals [Source: ev-1].

Judge Amit Mehta ruled on August 5, 2024, that these practices—specifically paying companies like Apple and Samsung billions of dollars to remain the default search engine—created a self-reinforcing loop where defaults generated scale, which produced data, improved quality, and protected the default position against rivals [Source: ev-1].
Evidence presented at trial showed that Google paid approximately $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021 and gave Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue [Source: ev-1].

Additionally, Google was prohibited from paying for default search placement or entering into revenue-sharing agreements, and it faces limits on acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1].
